survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The report is based on ICCS 2009’s two-stage cluster sampling design: schools were sampled with PPS (probability proportional to size using enrolled students), and within each sampled school an intact class from the target grade was randomly selected with all students in that class surveyed. Participation requirements were set at 85% for selected schools and 85% for selected students within schools (yielding a weighted overall participation rate of 75%), and the achieved student sample sizes are reported by country. The report presents results as national percentages and scale averages with standard errors, implying complex survey estimation consistent with ICCS procedures, but it does not name specific weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife). For secondary analysts using the ICCS international database, the recommended approach is to apply the provided student sampling weights and replicate weights (if available) to obtain correct standard errors under the clustered design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This report is primarily a descriptive and comparative large-scale assessment report using ICCS scaling outputs (Rasch-based scale scores and Warm’s weighted likelihood estimates) and item-level percentages, rather than an empirical predictive modeling study that would require explicit plausible-value (PV) handling documentation. PVs are not the focus of the analysis pipeline described here; instead, the report discusses scaling and standardized scale metrics for civic knowledge and questionnaire constructs. Missing-data handling is not specified in the provided text, which is typical for official assessment reports that rely on IEA/OECD/IEA processing pipelines documented elsewhere (e.g., the ICCS technical report).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The target student population was lower-secondary students in Grade 8 (approximately age 14) provided the average age in Grade 8 was at least 13.5 years; otherwise Grade 9 became the target population. Within each participating school, an intact class from the target grade was randomly selected and all students in that class were surveyed. The report also notes that in Chile and parts of Colombia data collection occurred Oct–Dec 2008, while other countries and the other part of Colombia occurred Feb–May 2009; Guatemala and Paraguay were assessed at the beginning of the new school year when students were already in Grade 9. Coverage and exclusions from the target population are reported in Appendix A (e.g., school-level and within-sample exclusions), and participation thresholds were applied (85% schools and 85% students within schools; weighted overall participation 75%).

data.outcome_summary: ICCS 2009 Latin American Report summarizes results from the Latin American regional module of the International Civic and Citizenship Education Study (ICCS 2009) for six participating countries (Chile, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Guatemala, Mexico, Paraguay). The student assessment combined an international civic knowledge test (80 items; 79 used for scaling) with a Latin American regional cognitive test (16 multiple-choice items) administered after the international test; students also completed international and Latin American questionnaires. Civic knowledge was scaled using Rasch modeling for the international test and calibrated regional items onto the international civic knowledge scale, with proficiency levels defined on the international metric (mean 500, SD 100; levels spanning 395–478, 479–562, and 563+). Questionnaire constructs were scaled using IRT (Rasch Partial Credit Model) and reported as standardized scale scores (mean 50, SD 10) for equally weighted regional databases. The report reports national percentages and scale averages (with standard errors) and compares Latin American averages to the international ICCS average, finding relatively low civic knowledge in the region and systematic associations between civic knowledge and attitudes toward authoritarianism, corruption, and disobeying the law, while also documenting empathy, identity, diversity attitudes, and reported aggression/violence experiences.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction treats the document as an official IEA assessment report rather than an empirical machine-learning paper. Consequently, there is no ML training/evaluation pipeline, no predictive target variable, and no reported PV-handling strategy in the sense required for ML predictive modeling. The report’s focus is on assessment design, scaling, and descriptive/comparative results across countries and subgroups, so fields like ml_techniques and main_findings are intentionally left empty.
